Chart of the Week: Routing Guide Premium, 2nd Tender, Routing Guide Acceptance Share for the first tender – USA SONAR : RGP2.USA, RGAS1.USA
The price of a rejected tender jumped this week. SONAR’s Routing Guide Premium for the 2nd tender (RGP2) climbed to 10.69% on Thursday, up 1.87 percentage points from 8.82% a week earlier and its highest reading since September. Meanwhile, the Routing Guide Acceptance Share for the 1st, or primary, tender (RGAS1) slid to 88.06%, down 88 basis points in a week and its lowest level since September.
Put simply, fewer loads are sticking with the primary carrier, and backup carriers are charging more to take them. Both moves landed in the run-up to Thanksgiving, when holiday freight typically starts to squeeze truckload capacity.
The routing guide premium measures the difference in cost between the primary carrier and the carriers further down a shipper’s routing guide. It is an all-in rate difference that includes fuel and accessorial charges.
Premiums move inversely to tender acceptance, and they tend to move slowly until they don’t. Sharp changes around holidays and market disruptions can blow up shippers’ contingency budgets.
Heading into this holiday period, shippers’ routing guides put the cost of a primary acceptance failure at around 8.8%. In about a week, that premium has jumped nearly 2 percentage points, and it will probably go higher. A year ago, a primary acceptance failure cost around 4%, and that premium expanded to around 8% by Christmas.
This rapid expansion in cost is a critical detail that many transportation managers miss when selecting providers and building routing guides. Secondary carriers typically feel the same capacity pressure as primary carriers. Because they are not a top priority for the shipper, the shipper is not a top priority for them. When the whole market is under pressure and spot rates are climbing, a carrier has little reason to haul freight below market rates for business it won’t keep once the market stabilizes.
Some of the increase comes from contract-plus pricing, in which the shipper adds an amount on top of the standard contract rate for the primary carrier. This keeps the shipper from having to turn to the spot market or ask a carrier unfamiliar with its freight to go out of its way, at a much higher cost to serve.
This premium does not show up directly in spot rates because the freight is not technically spot freight. Contract tenders have much longer lead times than spot loads, currently around 3.7 days versus roughly a single day. That often makes the contract market a leading indicator of market disruption.
As of Thursday, Nov. 19, shippers were already feeling the pain of deteriorating carrier compliance, even though spot rates, as measured by the National Truckload Index (NTI), were flat to slightly lower week over week. When spot rates rise quickly, the spot market can also pull capacity away from contract freight.
The main lesson from this chart is that shippers’ contingency carriers are not a given when the market turns volatile. The market sets the cost of service in those periods, but that cost should still be a discussion point in bid negotiations, because the relationship has to go beyond the paper. Carriers can’t be expected to ignore the market for a shipper that values their service only when it needs a backup.
About the Chart of the Week
The FreightWaves Chart of the Week is a chart selection from SONAR that provides an interesting data point to describe the state of the freight markets. A chart is chosen from thousands of potential charts on SONAR to help participants visualize the freight market in real time. Each week a Market Expert will post a chart, along with commentary, live on the front page. After that, the Chart of the Week will be archived on FreightWaves.com for future reference.
SONAR aggregates data from hundreds of sources, presenting the data in charts and maps and providing commentary on what freight market experts want to know about the industry in real time.
The FreightWaves data science and product teams are releasing new datasets each week and enhancing the client experience.

Rendering: How About That New Fiat Punto?
6 photos
Photo: Instagram | kdesignag
Chances are you do not care about the Fiat Punto if you live in the United States of America, but Europeans may want to pay attention to this model, as rumor has it that it might return from the dead.
Unofficial information speaks about a possible introduction at the end of 2027 or in 2028, though it has yet to be confirmed at this point. Such a thing could utilize Stellantis’ CMP/e-CMP construction, and this means that both internal combustion lumps and electric powertrains could be in the pipeline.
A brand-new Fiat Punto based on that platform would mean that the model would share its nuts and bolts with the Fiat 600, as well as the Citroen C4, DS 3 Crossback, Opel / Vauxhall Corsa, Mokka, Peugeot 208, 2008, and other similar models, including the Jeep Avenger. The Alfa Romeo Junior and the Lancia Ypsilon are also based on this construction.
Mind you, we haven’t kept the latter two for last for nothing, because some of their styling cues have inspired the model pictured in the gallery. This is nothing more than a mere rendering take on a hypothetical new-gen Fiat Punto, and for what it’s worth, nothing suggests that the actual car will look anything like this CGI project. But then again, a new Punto hasn’t been officially confirmed, as we already told you.
Photo: Instagram | kdesignag Signed by @kdesignag and shared on social media recently, this imagined new Fiat Punto looks more like a subcompact crossover than a traditional supermini. It has the company’s name on the grille, which is flanked by a pair of T-shaped headlights the remind us of certain Volvos, as well as extra DRLs on the sides of the bumper. T-shaped taillights can be seen at the rear, alongside a bumper that’s similar to the front one.
There is black plastic cladding on the lower parts of the body, including on the wheel arches, and these, as well as the generous ground clearance, as well as the car’s overall proportions, make it look more like a crossover. And that’s probably for the best, as traditional passenger cars, including subcompact hatchbacks, have lost traction to high-riding models.
As a reminder, Fiat made three generations of the Punto . The last one saw the light of day between 2004 and 2018 in Europe, and it was assembled not only in Italy, but also in India and Brazil. Giorgetto Giugiaro at Italdesign was responsible for sketching it out.
The model was offered as a hatch and a panel van, with a front-engine and front-wheel drive layout, and was based on the same construction as the era’s Linea, Fiorino, Alfa Romeo MiTo, and Opel Corsa (D). The powertrain family comprised numerous gasoline engines, as well as a CNG, and a few diesel units, and it varied from one market to the other. America’s heartland is full of rural communities that are miles away from its major cities, both geographically and culturally – but that doesn’t mean these more sparsely populated regions can’t reap the benefits of electrification. In fact, EVs offer rural drivers even more benefits than they do to city-dwellers!
UPDATE 21NOV2026 : this is an annual (ish) post I have been updating since 2024.
“An electric lifestyle would be a boon to our rural heartland,” wrote th e Union of Concerned Scientists’ Maria Cecilia Pinto de Moura . “Rural communities across the country have their own distinguishing characteristics, but certain shared characteristics such as driving distances, the type of vehicles driven, and socio-economics are factors which contribute to this larger potential to benefit from vehicle electrification.”
Pinto de Moura went on to outline five ways rural and country drivers could benefit from going electric – but that was in 2021, and a whole lot has changed in the nearly six years since. As such, I thought it was high time we revisit some of the reasons EVs are a great fit for rural lifestyles, see if we could uncover any new ones, and outline the reasons we think rural drivers should rush to embrace electric vehicles in the coming calendar year.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
1. More miles means more savings
David Blenkle’s 252,000 mile Mustang Mach-E; via Ford.
When you hear that line about, “the average American drives 30 to 40 miles a day,” remember that in towns like Wellington, Ohio, or Colfax, Washington, 30 miles is a grocery run. Each way. So when people trot out that old line about range anxiety , what rural drivers actually hear isn’t reassurance . It’s dismissal — a suggestion that they drive too far for an EV to work, when nothing could be further from the truth.
A recent study by Rural Climate Partnership found that rural drivers spend an average of 44% more on fuel than city dwellers, and that the top 3.6% of rural drivers — the “supermilers” who rack up the most miles — could save over $4,000 each year by switching to electric fuel.
2. Electric trucks have arrived
Sierra AT4 EV towing a boat; via GM.
Country guys and gals love their pickups, and arguably the biggest difference between the EV market of 2021 and 2027 is that electric trucks and SUVs are no longer a novelty. There are now battery-powered options ready to haul, handle chores, head out camping, and tow a trailer .
What’s more, a new wave of more affordable electric trucks from Ford , Slate , and others is challenging the idea that you need a $50,000 half-ton pickup to get real work done. Early interest suggests there’s plenty of pent-up demand for capable, accessible electric work trucks that don’t need to be twenty feet long or cost more than what your parent’s paid for their house .
3. Home charging just works
R1S home charging; via Rivian.
With only about 45% of rural counties having access to DC fast charging , public charging still isn’t as visible as many first-time EV buyers might like, but it’s far better than it used to be — and improving fast. Still, that’s not the real EV advantage. Home charging is .
Unlike many apartment-dwelling urban drivers, most rural owners can charge right at home. More than 80% of rural households have a driveway or garage that are ideal for overnight Level 2 charging, and many already have a 240V outlet, keeping setup costs ( if there even are any ) to a minimum.
Plug in before bed, wake up to a full battery every morning, and do it for pennies on the dollar, especially with off-peak rates.
4. Lifesaving battery power
F-150 Lightning plugged in; via Ford.
If disaster strikes and you lose power, your EV could be more than just a way to get around. Many electric cars and trucks have the ability to power refrigerators , freezers, well pumps, lights, and other household essentials for days , either through onboard outlets or a dedicated vehicle-to-home (V2H) system that feeds electricity directly into your home’s electrical panel. Ford’s from-the-ashes F-150 Lightning and Tesla’s Cybertruck are already among the EVs making that capability a reality, and newer, more affordable electric trucks promise to bring V2H tech to even more households.
If you live in an area prone to extreme weather, where severe storms, hurricanes, or wildfires can leave homes without electricity for days , that’s a pretty compelling benefit. Keeping food cold, medical equipment running or essential medication refrigerated can be a literal lifesaver – and your EV’s battery might be the biggest backup power source you own.
5. EVs are more affordable than ever
E-transit electric van; via Ford.
It’s been a few years since a working class guy could reasonably expect to get a new pickup for less than $50,000. And, while much has been made of the “high cost of electric vehicles,” the truth is that thanks to killer lease deals , new tax incentives , and companies like Ford Pro and TRC that are willing to help you find even more funding to help pay for them, EVs can often be had for less than a comparable gas model .
As such, getting behind the wheel of an ultra-powerful, ultra smooth-running electric pickup truck from your favorite brand is easier than ever.
6. Energy independence and American jobs
GM Defense electric military vehicle; via GM.
At the risk of sounding like a paranoid red hat, rural Americans are proud Americans – just like rural Canadians are proud Canadians . Unfortunately, every gallon of gas burned in their pickups and SUVs came from oil drilled, refined, and traded on global markets — and that means supporting the oil business and economies of nations whose values don’t always align with, or maybe are even outright hostile to theirs.
Switching to an EV can help more of that money right here at home, especially as more and better battery recycling efforts come online and newer battery and anode/cathode chemistries are developed, reducing dependence on rare Earth metals, cobalt, and even lithium.
Even better, thanks to the rapid expansion and dramatically reduced costs of wind and solar power , you can power your EV with energy that is 100% Made in the USA, that doesn’t support foreign oil interests or involve you in a bunch of dumb oil wars (except indirectly), and which creates good-paying construction and maintenance jobs for local workers .
7. Used EVs are cheaper than ever
Chevrolet Bolt EUV, via GM.
In my experience, rural buyers appreciate things that last, and are moved more by lasting quality than fleeting fashions – and that’s exactly why they should be looking at EVs .
We recently covered a 2019 Chevy Bolt that had put more than 470,000 miles on its odometer , along with data from Ford showing its battery packs maintain more than 90% of their battery health after 100,000 miles .
And while we’re talking about data, it should be noted that EVs aren’t some new, unknown technology. The first modern high-voltage car battery hit the road more than 30 years ago (the Prius was released in 1996, as a 1997 model). Some of those cars are still on the road – and there are literally tens of thousands of EVs out there still performing their daily driver duties every day.
What am I missing?
EV6 GT burnout; via Kia.
There are obviously more reasons to go electric than these, from lower cost of ownership to saving the planet to absolutely killer burnouts that would make the one-tire-fire era IROC Camaros hang their 305s in shame – but I think those kind of fade into the background as being appealing to just about everyone, instead of being especially appealing to rural drivers.

I live in rural Australia in a village that doesn't even have a fuel bowser. My shopping trip is usually around 164km (100miles). I have solar on my roof. I now have an EV (one of the Chinese brands that aren't available in the USA) and am delighted with it. I'm saving a lot of money on fuel and because the solar feed-in tariff goes negative in the middle of the day (I have to pay the utility company to take my electricity) by charging the car at home I save money there. For rural people with roof space for solar EVs should be a no-brainer, but like many rural areas my district is incredibly conservative (do a search for Barnaby Joyce, my local member) and the populace are convinced they don't drive far enough, they'll catch on fire (mine has an LFP battery, so the risk is low) and that I'll need to replace the battery in a year (even though the battery has an 8 year warranty).

EICMA 2026 • Here Are Some of the Serious and Obscure Brands That EICMA 2026 Had To Offer – Worth Knowing About
Mom's First Car Spent 30 Years in the Garage, Now She Wants To See Her Son Driving It
15 photos
Photo: WD Detailing | YouTube
This 42-year-old Volkswagen Scirocco spent 30 years locked inside a garage. Its owner got it from her mom, but life happened, and she just stopped driving it at some point. Now, with a son passionate about cars from the 1980s, she wants to pass it on to him. But first, it needs to be cleaned up and fixed.
Juliet remembers that her parents bought the 1984 Volkswagen Scirocco almost new in 1985 after it had served as a demo car at the dealership. Juliet’s mom drove it quite a lot in the 1980s. It meant the world to her. When Juliet turned 16, she passed it on to her daughter.
When Juliet's mom passed away, her father couldn't let the car go. So he parked it, and nobody ever touched it again. Years passed, and Juliet’s first car is still parked in the family garage. It doesn't run, it doesn't drive, and it is covered in a thick layer of dust and grime.
Juliet’s son is now 25, and she would love to give him a chance to drive it. So she called the detailers to wash 30 years of neglect off her first car. But it won't be easy. The car is sitting on four tires that were slashed at some point. Some kids from the neighborhood did it when Juliet’s mother was in hospice.
Photo: WD Detailing | YouTube RJ of WD Detailing trailers the Scirocco to the studio, and surprisingly, with a bit of starting fluid sprayed into the intake, the engine fires up right away, but it dies right out. A mechanic will take care of that later. Now, the first step is removing the wheels, but RJ needs Miss Persuasion, which is actually a sledgehammer, to help him hammer the wheels off.
Then vacuuming is the next step before the power wash. But as water makes the dirt collected over three decades vanish, it reveals the poor condition of the silver paint. RJ uses a degreaser to lift years of grime off the 42-year-old paint, which has become very vulnerable. Rust has bitten chunks out of the doors and fenders.
The interior tells the exact same story. The one who cleans it up is Mike, who owns a Scirocco himself. His is a 16-valve 1987 unit, looking like it just rolled off the production line. This is what he wants to see in the silver 1984 Scirocco with a blue interior, entirely covered in grime and dust that it has collected over the years.
And it’s not just the grime and dust. Mike is sure that mice have built a home on board the Volkswagen and is determined to find it. While searching for the mice, he found an old Pepsi can and a Tropicana juice bottle from the early 1990s.
Photo: WD Detailing | YouTube The Compressed air and the vacuum cleaner, the stain extractor, and the steamer won’t work miracles on a carpet that mice had their fair share of fun with. So it needs to come out. Otherwise, the Scirocco would be a rolling biohazard. The detailers scrub every single inch underneath it.
Popping the hood reveals how years have taken their toll on the car. The insulation is disintegrating the moment RJ steers his vacuum cleaner toward it. The engine bay is just as bad. It contains 30 years of oil leaks and fluid spills, which make the detailer label it a disaster zone. He has to clean it up before Aki, the mechanic, arrives at the scene. He is well aware that one wrong move and the car, with all the wires and hoses exposed, might never start again.
At least not with this engine under the hood. The 1984 Volkswagen Scirocco came with a 1.8-liter inline-four with mechanical fuel injection, producing 90 horsepower (91 metric horsepower) and 100 pound-feet (136 Newton meters) of torque for a top speed of 111 mph (178 kph).
RJ lets his citrus degreaser do its job before he rinses it off and prepares the territory for Aki, the 21-year-old mechanic who is half the age of the car, to do more than just make the inline-four run for a few seconds like they did the moment they rolled the car off the trailer into their studio.
Photo: WD Detailing | YouTube To access the fuel pump and see the condition it is in, he needs to remove the rear seats. It needs to be replaced. Three days later, when the new one arrives, they realize they waited three days only to find out they ordered the wrong pump.
The bad news is that mice even made a nest on top of the fuel injection system. But he can deal with that. He also needed to deal with a rusty fuel tank. Replacing it was not an option, so he came up with a fuel cell in the trunk. Now, $2,000 later, when the inline-four fires up, it doesn’t shut down instantly. It idles and sounds like "your grandpa's tractor," Aki says.
So now, RJ can take it back to Juliet, who is waiting in the company of her son. The young man has never seen the Volkswagen Scirocco running and driving. Juliet can’t believe her ears when she hears the engine.
" You are a miracle worker ," she tells RJ as she applauds his work. A few days before, the car was just a big mouse nest. Now, it looks like it has never even sat parked, untouched for 30 years.

This Gorgeous Tiny House from Tasmania Hides the Most Unique Vintage Finds
34 photos
Photo: Artisan Tiny Homes
To simply say that the Little Keepsake is beautiful would be an understatement. A treasure trove of real vintage finds, personal items from the owner’s previous residences, and impeccable contemporary styling, this Tasmanian tiny house goes far beyond the concept of custom design. This is tiny house styling and craftsmanship at its finest, with the kind of inherent warmth and individuality that outshine all conventional luxury.
There’s really nothing out there quite like the Little Keepsake – more than a spectacular house on wheels, built and styled with stunning attention to detail, this unique abode is like a living museum and art gallery designed to give certain precious objects a second life. Just as its lovely name suggests, this custom tiny house is filled with objects that the owner had enjoyed previously and didn’t want to let go, as well as authentic vintage finds.
Many tiny homes try to replicate a vintage aesthetic through style choices, but the Little Keepsake incorporates actual vintage items and repurposed objects into what can be described as an impeccable contemporary style. In other words, this house is by no means a messy collection of “old” things, scattered around a cramped interior – it’s a luxurious home equipped with modern conveniences, ready for comfortable living, and furnished impeccably.
Photo: Artisan Tiny Homes “A tiny home that celebrates imperfection, history, and individuality” – this is how its builder, the family-owned Artisan Tiny Homes, based, in Wivenhoe, Tasmania, describes it. It all started with a customer who wanted to find a new home not just for themselves, but for their personal collection as well. That is how, although brand-new, this tiny house ended up hiding more exciting vintage finds than a museum on wheels, masterfully integrated throughout.
Even from the outside, the contemporary-style corrugated metal exterior with timber insertions gently incorporates vintage windows. A striking bright green door hints at the home’s artistic and quirky interior, while elegant French back doors provide a second entrance. Inside, guests will discover a unique mix of old, repurposed doors (several of them), stained glass accents (a beautiful artistic touch), and old timber items everywhere.
Perhaps one of the most spectacular things about Little Keepsake is that it doesn’t just pack a selection of vintage and repurposed objects in the lounge, for instance. Just like a treasure trove, every single area is worth exploring, in order to discover the “secret” vintage finds. It even has one of the most beautiful bathrooms, by far, you’ll ever see in a tiny house, and there are statement pieces in almost every part of the house.
Photo: Artisan Tiny Homes On the ground floor, an open living room is flanked by the kitchen and the bathroom, while both lofts serve as spacious bedrooms. Benefitting from a nine-meter (29.5 feet) length and a height of slightly over four meters (13 feet), this gooseneck-type home on wheels boasts ample floor space for a full-size kitchen, a spectacular bathroom, and two comfortable bedrooms in the loft area. Each loft includes staircase access, making this home a lot more comfortable for full-time living.
Little Keepsake has the dimensions, the functionality, and the thoughtful layout of an ideal family home. One of its main attractions is the huge U-shaped kitchen, which incorporates a classic Australian breakfast bar – large and strategically placed under a big window, as well as gorgeous cabinetry throughout.
The pastel green shade of the cabinets was chosen for its “gentle country feel”, and it complements the natural tone and texture of the timber countertops beautifully. The massive, copper sink is an absolute statement piece, coupled with vintage-style tapware and brightly-patterned fabrics for contrast.
Photo: Artisan Tiny Homes Full-size, premium appliances bring this kitchen into modern times, as well as the black-framed windows all-around that ingeniously mimic a panoramic effect. Filled with natural light, perfectly spacious for a family, and furnished with that custom cabinetry that provides ample storage space, this farmhouse-inspired kitchen feels almost cinematic.
The lounge itself is no more than a spacious transition area, big enough to fit a full-size sofa with a generous view thanks to the French doors, but the staircases are enough to elevate this entire space on their own. Especially the one close to the kitchen area, which leads to the main bedroom, is a true work of art. It displays timber spindles in various finishes and colors, which are actually vintage items in their original form.
Built-in storage is also elegantly incorporated into this staircase, and the interior design is further enriched with old stained glass accents high above the entrance door, plus a superb bespoke chandelier in a shade that of vibrant green that matches the kitchen cabinetry. Every single detail is impeccably integrated for a seamless look, where old meets new in a sophisticated way.
Photo: Artisan Tiny Homes The other staircase is conventionally-built, but it also hides a little vintage perk: another repurposed metal rod that becomes a practical handrail, in sharp contrast to the white, farmhouse-inspired staircase. Another statement piece that adds character to the lounge is the beautiful bathroom door – not inspired by, but an actual, old barn door that was reclaimed and given a second life.
Behind this heavy timber door, you’ll find one of the most unique, sophisticated tiny house bathrooms. A stunning copper sink takes center stage, paired perfectly with an old timber vanity, and vintage-style tapware. In sharp contrast, the shower cabin is luxuriously contemporary, a well-blended mix of green tiles and glass panels. All the storage space, including a dedicated laundry nook, is custom-built.
Upstairs, in the main loft, guests will also be delighted to discover custom-built wardrobes that look absolutely beautiful: emerald green adorned with vintage-style doorknobs and matching patterned wallpaper. The floor space of this walk-through loft bedroom has been wisely used to fit in those large custom cabinets, in addition to the queen-sized bed. A vintage swing door adds the right vintage accents, and large windows bring in natural light.
Photo: Artisan Tiny Homes The second loft is smaller, it only has a vintage nightstand as storage furniture, but what makes it extra comfortable are the numerous large windows, coupled with another big, vertical window at the top of the staircase.
Flooring throughout is waterproof laminate, and the house is equipped to be connected to all regular utilities. Perfect for accommodating up to four people, Little Keepsake is an excellent choice for families (a similar platform can be used for other builds, but this Tasmanian tiny house builder only does custom tiny homes.)
Little Keepsake’s uniqueness is the result of a visionary customer and a talented builder joining forces. Kerrie, the soul and force behind Artisan Tiny Homes, is an interior designer and an artist, which explains the stunning beauty of all the abodes rolled out from this workshop. Working with her husband Kevin, who is a builder and a restorer, and with their daughter who is a carpenter, Kerrie brings to life true works of art on wheels, unlike anything else on the market.
Photo: Artisan Tiny Homes Artisan Tiny Homes was established almost a decade ago, in 2018, and since then it has delivered just a little over 30 tiny homes, because it’s not about quantity and mass market, but about bringing art, soul, and craftsmanship into bespoke homes. I almost can’t imagine any of the owners of an Artisan tiny home selling their homes, precisely because they’re so unique and filled with passion in every detail – and that’s how it should be.

This Ashben Conversions Camper Van Is a Head-Turner Outside and a Refined Retreat Inside
16 photos
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Ashben Conversions
It's incredible what some specialized camper van builders can do when working with the limited interior real estate offered by vans. Thanks to efficient, clever designs, a camper van can be almost as well-equipped as a tiny studio apartment – take this rig as an example.
What we have here is a conversion based on a MAN TGE. It was created by Ashben Conversions, a Sheffield, UK-based company specializing in high-quality camper vans and motorhomes.
This rig was built by Ashben as a ready-to-go inventory van, and was sold completed to a customer who was able to skip the conversion wait list. As always, let's begin by taking a look at the exterior.
For starters, the vehicle is a head-turner thanks to its exterior look. It's finished in Crayon Grey paint and has several black exterior mods , as well as a small black decal with white geometric lines.
The vehicle rides on 20-inch Riviera wheels wrapped in General Grabber all-terrain tires. On top of the rig, Ashben fitted a Thule 6300 awning, a Heki roof vent, two Maxxair vent fans, and a 250 W solar panel.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Ashben Conversions Other notable mods include power and water hookups, an outdoor shower connection, an access door for the toilet waste, and a set of flares.
Flares, also known as pods or capsules, are designed to increase the van width to allow you to arrange a bed inside east to west instead of the standard north to south. This rig's CJL side pods are color matched to the van's paint and come with half-slider windows.
Inside is where things get interesting. You'll be greeted by a modern, well-crafted interior with a variety of comforts. It has an open layout, with no wall separating the driver's cabin from the living space.
Regarding aesthetics, you'll notice cabinetry with a darker grain finish, grey Alcantara upholstery for the walls, and a ceiling finished in grey woven fabric, complete with three long recessed LED light strips. The look is complemented by white solid surface countertops and a variety of black accents, such as black leather upholstery and black hardware.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Ashben Conversions The driver and passenger seats are mounted on swivel bases, allowing you to turn them around to face the back of the van. The front part of the interior can double as a seating area for after you set up camp, especially since you get a table that can be reached from either seat.
The seating area continues further back in the form of a dual bench seat complete with seat belts. There's also a cabinet above offering a decent amount of storage space.
Next, we have the kitchen on the passenger side, by the sliding door. It features a deep stainless steel sink with a cover, a single-burner induction stovetop, a microwave oven, and a fridge with a tiny freezer compartment.
A sizeable overhead cabinet, four drawers, and a cabinet underneath the sink are available for storage in the kitchen.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Ashben Conversions Most high-end camper vans come with one of the most sought-after camper van facilities: a bathroom. This van's bathroom sits opposite the kitchen, hidden behind a tall standard door.
It boasts a stainless steel tray, a bench toilet that can be emptied from the outside, and a shower with a handheld wand. I'm also fond of the bathroom's look, with a concrete effect paired with black fixtures.
The rear part of the living space is taken up by a fixed sleeping arrangement with a double-sized bed that's 6'4" (193 centimeters) long. The bedroom also offers a Maxxair vent fan above, two overhead cabinets, two reading lights, and a small open cupboard.
Finally, we have the garage underneath the bedroom, accessible from both inside and outside the van. It provides abundant room for storage and accommodates part of the utility systems inside two boxes on the sides.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Ashben Conversions The builders installed gas struts, which make it easier for you to open the rear doors and prevent them from slamming shut or hitting the vehicle's body.
Power is on the left side – the electrical system's highlights are a 460 Ah Fogstar battery bank and a 3,000 W Victron inverter/charger. Three charging sources are available: solar power , shore power, and DC-DC charging while the engine is running. If you use them correctly, you might just never run out of juice while traveling.
As for plumbing, the van is equipped with a 10-liter (2.6-gallon) Propex water heater and two tanks for fresh and grey water – both are mounted underneath the vehicle.
The last important system in this rig is a diesel-powered Webasto heater that's tapped directly into the vehicle's fuel tank.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Ashben Conversions All in all, Ashben Conversions created a comfortable and travel-ready mobile home with an enviable blend of practicality and aesthetics. Unfortunately, we don't know how much this van cost, but the company offers a configurator that lets you easily customize your dream build and find out a price estimate for it.

Volkswagen Beetle Returns Once Again, This Time as an ID. Series Model in Hot Hatchback CGI Form
8 photos
Photo: augusto_fuchsdesign / Instagram
The Volkswagen Beetle is probably one of the most important automobiles of all time, especially the original series which ran from 1938 until 2003 for no less than 65 years. It’s really no wonder that Volkswagen tried to continue in its spirit with two modern incarnations, right?
Officially known as the Volkswagen Type 1 , the Beetle was a small family car with a distinctive bug-like design, which over the years brought it universal recognition and numerous nicknames, plus over 21.5 million sales. Since it was only offered as a single generation, the production time of 65 years even today stands as a record, by the way.
Volkswagen tried to recapture its popularity and colloquial spirit with the Volkswagen New Beetle produced from 1997 through 2011 and then again made another attempt with the A5 version until 2019. It wasn’t meant to be, as none of these versions achieved the success of their illustrious predecessor, and VW decided to stop trying to offer a retro model akin to the likes of the MINI Cooper, for example.
On the other hand, nowadays it seems there’s a growing roster of EV hot hatchbacks around the world, including the newly released Volkswagen ID. Polo GTI, but also the likes of the Hyundai Ioniq 5 N, MINI John Cooper Works Electric, Abarth 500e and 600e, plus the Alpine A290, which is based on the retro-modern Renault 5 E-Tech.
As such, it’s really no wonder that someone thought about this niche for a potential fourth outing of the iconic Volkswagen Beetle – and since that person is a member of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators, they also did something about it rather than just dwelling aimlessly across the parallel universes of vehicular CGI.
Meet Augusto Fuchs, aka ' augusto_fuchsdesign ' on social media, who is a Transportation Design Master at IED Torino and Surface Modeler & Designer for Airbus Helicopters, and their most recent unofficial, hypothetical design project: the VW ID. Beetle Beast. It should be a part of the novel ID. series, which includes novelties like the Volkswagen ID. Polo, Cross, and Tiguan , but it would obviously act as the hero model tasked with bringing enthusiasts to the brand.
The credentials are unchanged for the modern revival – it’s still a bug-like model with a distinctive silhouette and signature round headlights, but now it would probably make not just the small EV hot hatchbacks feel uncomfortable next to it but also frighten the larger models like the popular Hyundai Ioniq 5 N.
It’s also clearly a specialist car, with room for just four on board due to the arching roofline and packing all the aerodynamic goodies of the late 2020s, including a widebody kit and massive aero elements like the front splitters and the humongous diffuser plus wing around the back. Audi Concept Q Virtually Reinterprets the Original Audi Quattro for the New Age of Electrification
20 photos
Photo: angelodilor_design / Instagram
The Ingolstadt-based automaker hasn’t been feeling all too well over the past couple of years, with dwindling sales across the globe and massive drops in places that count more than others in the grand scheme of things – like North America.
Hopefully, things are going to change going into 2027, as the company has just about anything for everyone across the board, from the recently relaunched Audi A2, which came back to life just as quirky but as an e-tron model, right up to the new hero supercar , the Audi Nuvolari.
More importantly, there is also cool stuff in between them for the North American market, such as the all-new Audi A6 Allroad, which is a worthy mid-size station wagon alternative to crossover SUVs, while the brand also doesn’t neglect the latter thanks to the newly introduced third-generation Audi Q7 and its first-ever Audi Q9 sibling with three rows of seats and flagship credentials worthy of a clash with the likes of the Cadillac Escalade and especially the BMW X7 and Mercedes-Benz GLS.
As such, it’s no wonder that everyone – including the rumor mill and the members of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators dwelling across the parallel universes of vehicular CGI- is keeping an eye on them. For example, just recently, Angelo Di Lorenzi, a former Exterior Design intern at Alfa Romeo and now a Junior Exterior Designer known as ' angelodilor_design ' on social media, envisioned the potential new-age return of the iconic Audi Quattro road and rally car.
It’s not a typo – Audi decided to rename its quattro four-wheel-drive system with all small letters in honor of the Audi Quattro, which launched at the 1980 Geneva Motor Show, almost three decades ago, as a model that sought to take advantage of the new rally rules of the era that finally allowed the use of four-wheel drive in competition racing. Dubbed the Audi Ur-Quattro, aka the primordial quattro model, the two-door coupe remains an important part of Audi’s modern legacy.
It also helped that it had a particular design, with the model related but not akin to the B2 Audi 80 compact executive sedan. Anyway, now the pixel master wants to show us their “personal vision of the next chapter in the Audi Quattro story, exploring how its distinctive proportions, strong character, and rally heritage could be reinterpreted through a design approach that balances the original’s bold identity with a more contemporary aesthetic.”
This means that the CGI expert keeps the defining signature traits of the original Audi Quattro, like the fastback shape and the square headlight style, along with the full-width black treatment of the taillights, which were actually connected by a styling element, not fully lit. But, of course, now it’s all mixed with contemporary widebody attire and slim LED elements, both at the front and around the back. As a red wave of Chinese-built electric vehicles breaks over Europe and Canada, Xiaomi is selling its electric cars outside of China for the first time ever – and its starting its push for global growth with the UAE in 2027.
Xiaomi is selling its electrified vehicles to buyers outside of China for first time this week, with the SU7 sedan, YU7 crossover , and Skynomad SUV now listed for sale throughout the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The company isn’t going it alone, however.
Xiomi is working local distributor Gargash Prime Automotive, rather than operating its own retail network, with Xiaomi CEO Lei Jun confirming that the company would officially enter Western car markets next year at the APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen held 17NOV .
CarNewsChina reports that Gargash Prime Automotive is offering 13 variants across the Xiaomi SU7 sedan, YU7 SUV , and Skynomad extended-range electric SUV lineup, with retail prices starting at 169,900 AED ($~46,200 US) for the SU7 Standard and climbing all the way up to 375,900 AED ($~102,000 US) for the range-topping SU7 Ultra.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Supercar Mecca
SU7 Ultra prototype; by Xiaomi.
Not to lump a bunch of nations with their own rich heritage and car culture together, but it’s fair to say that drivers in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Kuwait love their supercars – a nd the brand’s Xiaomi SU7 Ultra might be one of the most super of them all , thanks to fully 1,548 hp from three high-torque electric motors, the SU7 Ultra can sprint from 0-100 km/h (62 mph) in under two seconds on its way to a towering, 217 mph top speed.
It’s not just a straight-line speed machine, either. Xiaomi gave its go-fast flagship a serious track-focused makeover on its way to becomig the “Utlra,” complete with carbon-ceramic brakes, an aggressive ( if controversial ) composite aero package, an enormous rear wing, and a chassis tuned to tackle the turns the Green Hell of the Nürburgring .
And, at a relatively reasonable $102,000 equivalent price, I’d be willing to bet that a lot of the hypercar-loving Emiratis will be eager to get their hands on one.
The first customer deliveries of the Xiaomi SU7 Standard and Ultra, YU7 Standard, and Skynomad N70 Pro models are scheduled for December of this year, with deliveries of the remaining variants scheduled for February 2027.
